results.question: How do you initialize a new Git repository in an existing directory?
results.expected_answer: To turn a directory into a new Git repository, you run the command git init. This command creates a .git directory where Git stores all the project's metadata and object database.
results.rtfm_answer: To initialize a new Git repository in an existing directory, navigate to the project directory and run `git init`. This command creates a new `.git` subdirectory containing the necessary repository files, though nothing in the project is tracked yet at this point. [Source 1]

results.question: How do you get a copy of an existing Git repository from a server?
results.expected_answer: You use the git clone command to receive a full copy of nearly all data the server has for that project. Unlike other version control systems, Git receives every version of every file for the history of the project by default.
results.rtfm_answer:
To get a copy of an existing Git repository from a server, you use the `git clone` command followed by the URL of the repository. For example:

```console
$ git clone https://github.com/libgit2/libgit2
```

This command creates a new directory, initializes a `.git` directory inside it, pulls down all the data for the repository, and checks out the latest version. If you want to clone the repository into a different directory, you can specify the new directory name as an additional argument:

```console
$ git clone https://github.com/libgit2/libgit2 mylibgit
```

results.question: What command is used to check which files are in which state within your working directory?
results.expected_answer: The git status command shows you which files are modified but unstaged, which are staged for the next commit, and which are untracked. It also provides hints on how to move files between these states.
results.rtfm_answer: The `git status` command is used to check which files are in which state within your working directory. It shows the different states of files, including which are modified and unstaged, and which are staged but not yet committed.

results.question: How do you record staged snapshots permanently to the Git history?
results.expected_answer: The git commit command takes the files exactly as they are in the staging area and stores that snapshot permanently in the Git directory. Each commit also stores metadata such as the author's name, email, and a commit message.
results.rtfm_answer: To record staged snapshots permanently to the Git history, you perform a commit. This command takes the files as they are in the staging area and stores that snapshot permanently to your Git directory. [Source 1]

results.question: What is the command to stage changes for the next commit?
results.expected_answer: The git add command adds content from the working directory into the staging area, also known as the index. This allows you to selectively craft what your next commit snapshot will look like.
results.rtfm_answer: The command to stage changes for the next commit is `git add`. This command adds content from the working directory into the staging area for the next commit. [Source 1]

results.question: What is the technical definition of a branch in Git?
results.expected_answer: A branch in Git is simply a lightweight, movable pointer to one of the commits in your history. The default branch name created by git init is master.
results.rtfm_answer: In Git, a branch is a lightweight movable pointer to one of these commits. The default branch name is `master`, but it is exactly like any other branch. Every time you commit, the `master` branch pointer moves forward automatically. [Source 4]

results.question: How do you create a new branch without switching to it?
results.expected_answer: You can create a new branch pointer using the git branch command followed by the branch name. This creates a new pointer to the same commit you are currently on.
results.rtfm_answer: You can create a new branch without switching to it using the command `git branch <branch-name>`. This creates a new branch but keeps you on the current branch. [Source 2]

results.question: How do you switch from your current branch to another existing branch?
results.expected_answer: The git checkout command is used to switch to an existing branch. When you switch branches, Git reverts the files in your working directory to look like they did the last time you committed on that branch.
results.rtfm_answer:
To switch from your current branch to another existing branch, you use the `git checkout` command followed by the name of the branch you want to switch to. For example:

```console
$ git checkout another-branch
```

This command moves `HEAD` to point to the `another-branch` branch.

results.question: What is a shortcut command to create a new branch and switch to it immediately?
results.expected_answer: You can use the git checkout command with the -b switch to create a new branch and switch to it at the same time. This is a very common operation used when starting work on a new topic or issue.
results.rtfm_answer: The shortcut command to create a new branch and switch to it immediately is `git checkout -b new-branch`. This command combines the actions of creating a new branch and switching to it in one step. [Source 1]

results.question: What does the special HEAD pointer represent in Git?
results.expected_answer: In Git, HEAD is a special pointer that refers to the local branch you are currently working on. It serves as the parent of the next commit you create.
results.rtfm_answer: In Git, the HEAD pointer represents the current branch you are working on. It is a special pointer that moves as you make new commits, always pointing to the latest commit on the current branch. [Source 1] Additionally, HEAD can be a symbolic reference to the branch you're currently on, or it can contain the SHA-1 value of a Git object, such as when you check out a tag or a specific commit. [Source 2]

results.question: What happens during a fast-forward merge?
results.expected_answer: A fast-forward merge occurs when the commit you are merging in is a direct descendant of the commit you are currently on. Git simply moves the branch pointer forward because there is no divergent work to merge together.
results.rtfm_answer: During a fast-forward merge, Git moves the branch pointer forward to a commit that is reachable from the current branch tip. This happens when the merge base is directly on the current branch, and there is no divergent work to merge. Essentially, Git simplifies the merge by updating the branch pointer to the latest commit, as there are no conflicting changes to integrate. [Source 1]

results.question: How do you merge another branch into your currently checked-out branch?
results.expected_answer: To integrate changes, you use the git merge command followed by the name of the branch you wish to merge in. If the histories have diverged, Git performs a three-way merge using a common ancestor.
results.rtfm_answer:
To merge another branch into your currently checked-out branch, you use the `git merge` command followed by the name of the branch you want to merge. For example, if you want to merge the `iss53` branch into your current branch, you would run:

```sh
git merge iss53
```

This command will merge the specified branch into the branch you have checked out, creating a new merge commit if necessary.

results.question: What is unique about a merge commit compared to a normal commit?
results.expected_answer: A merge commit is special because it has more than one parent. It represents a snapshot that results from a three-way merge of different development lines.
results.rtfm_answer: A merge commit has more than one parent, distinguishing it from a normal commit which has only one parent. This special structure allows Git to incorporate changes from multiple branches into a single commit. [Source 1]

results.question: What occurs if you change the same part of the same file differently in two branches being merged?
results.expected_answer: Git will encounter a merge conflict and will not be able to merge the branches cleanly. It adds conflict markers to the affected files and requires the user to resolve the differences manually before committing.
results.rtfm_answer: If you change the same part of the same file differently in two branches being merged, Git will encounter a merge conflict. Git will pause the merge process and require you to resolve the conflict manually. You can see this in the example where `git merge iss53` results in a conflict in `index.html`, and you need to fix the conflicts and then commit the result. [Source 2]

results.question: What is the process of rebasing in Git?
results.expected_answer: Rebasing involves taking all the changes that were committed on one branch and replaying them on top of another branch. This operation rewinds the head to a common ancestor, saves diffs as temporary patches, and applies them in order on the target branch.
results.rtfm_answer: In Git, rebasing is the process of taking the changes introduced by commits on one branch and applying them on top of another branch. This is done using the `git rebase` command, which essentially cherry-picks each commit from the source branch and reapplies them to the target branch, starting from a common ancestor. This can be useful for maintaining a linear commit history.

results.question: What is the primary risk of rebasing commits that have been pushed publicly?
results.expected_answer: The golden rule of rebasing is to never rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that others may have based work on. Rebasing rewritten history that has been shared causes major confusion for collaborators who must then re-merge their own work.
results.rtfm_answer: The primary risk of rebasing commits that have been pushed publicly is that others may have based their work on those commits. If you then rewrite those commits with `git rebase` and push them up again, your collaborators will have to re-merge their work, leading to messy history when you try to pull their work back into yours. [Source 1]

results.question: How can you stop a rebase that is in progress and return to your original state?
results.expected_answer: If a rebase becomes too complex or you decide it was a mistake, you can run git rebase --abort. This returns your repository to the exact state it was in before the rebase command was started.
results.rtfm_answer: To stop a rebase that is in progress and return to your original state, you can use the command `git rebase --abort`. This will revert your repository to the state it was in before you started the rebase. [Source 1]

results.question: What is one major benefit of rebasing over merging when integrating changes?
results.expected_answer: Rebasing produces a cleaner, linear project history because it makes parallel work appear as if it happened in series. This is often preferred by project maintainers so they can integrate patches with a simple fast-forward.
results.rtfm_answer: One major benefit of rebasing over merging when integrating changes is that rebasing creates a cleaner history, making it appear as if all the work happened in series, even when it originally happened in parallel. [Source 1]

results.question: How do you register a new remote repository handle for your project?
results.expected_answer: You use the git remote add command followed by a shortname and the URL of the repository. This allows you to reference that URL easily using the shortname on the command line.
results.rtfm_answer:
To register a new remote repository handle for your project, you can use the `git remote add` command followed by the shortname and the URL of the remote repository. For example:

```sh
$ git remote add pb https://github.com/paulboone/ticgit
```

This command adds a new remote repository under the shortname `pb`, allowing you to reference it easily in commands like `git fetch pb`.

results.question: What is the difference between fetching and pulling from a remote?
results.expected_answer: The git fetch command downloads all data from a remote project that you don't have yet but does not automatically merge it with your work. The git pull command is a combination of fetching and then automatically merging that remote data into your current branch.
results.rtfm_answer: Fetching and pulling both involve communicating with a remote repository, but they differ in their actions. `git fetch` retrieves new data from the remote repository and stores it in your local database without merging it into your current branch. On the other hand, `git pull` fetches from the remote and then immediately tries to merge the fetched data into your current branch [Source 1: progit.pdf].

results.question: How do you push your local branch changes to a remote repository?
results.expected_answer: You use the command git push <remote> <branch> to share your commits. This only works if you have write access to the server and if no one else has pushed changes since your last fetch.
results.rtfm_answer:
To push your local branch changes to a remote repository, use the `git push` command followed by the name of the remote and the name of the branch. For example:

```console
$ git push origin master
```

This command pushes your local `master` branch to the `origin` remote repository. If you want to set up the branch to be pushed automatically with `git pull`, you can use the `--set-upstream` option:

```console
$ git push --set-upstream origin master
```

results.question: What are remote-tracking branches?
results.expected_answer: Remote-tracking branches are local references that represent the state of branches on a remote repository at the time of your last communication. They act as bookmarks to remind you where the remote branches were last seen.
results.rtfm_answer: Remote-tracking branches are branches that your local repository maintains to reflect the branches in a remote repository. They are used to show which remote branches you don’t yet have, which remote branches have been removed from the server, and to track the state of branches when you run commands like `git pull` and `git push`. [Source 1]

results.question: What are the three main sections of a Git project that files reside in?
results.expected_answer: Files in a Git project exist in the working tree, the staging area (also called the index), and the Git directory. The working tree is your local sandbox, the index stores information for the next commit, and the Git directory holds the metadata and object database.
results.rtfm_answer: I don't have enough information in the documentation to answer that question. The provided context does not specify the three main sections of a Git project where files reside.

results.question: What are the three types of objects Git stores in its object database?
results.expected_answer: Git's core data store consists of blobs, trees, and commits. Blobs represent file contents, trees represent directory structures and filenames, and commits store metadata and pointers to the root trees.
results.rtfm_answer: Git stores three types of objects in its object database: blobs, trees, and commits. Tags are also stored as objects, but they generally point to a commit rather than being a different type of object. [Source 1]

results.question: How does Git use the SHA-1 hash for data integrity?
results.expected_answer: Git checksums everything before it is stored and refers to it by that 40-character hexadecimal SHA-1 hash. This makes it impossible to change file or directory contents without Git detecting the corruption or change.
results.rtfm_answer: Git uses SHA-1 hashes to ensure data integrity by checksumming the contents of files and directories. When you add content to Git, it calculates a SHA-1 hash of the content, which is then used to name the file storing that content in the Git object database. This means that any change to the content would result in a different hash, allowing Git to detect and prevent data corruption or loss [Source 1].

results.question: What is the purpose of the Git 'index'?
results.expected_answer: The index, also known as the staging area, is a file that stores information about what will go into your next commit. It acts as a proposed next commit snapshot that Git looks at when you run the commit command.
results.rtfm_answer: The Git index, also known as the staging area, is where Git stores information about what will go into your next commit. It acts as a temporary storage space between your working directory and the object database. Changes made in the working directory can be selectively staged into the index before being committed permanently.

results.question: What are 'plumbing' and 'porcelain' commands in Git?
results.expected_answer: Porcelain commands are the user-friendly subcommands like checkout or branch that users use daily. Plumbing commands are lower-level subcommands designed to be chained together or used in scripts to perform fundamental operations.
results.rtfm_answer: In Git, 'plumbing' commands are lower-level, more complex commands designed to be used as building blocks for new tools and custom scripts. They give you access to the inner workings of Git. In contrast, 'porcelain' commands are more user-friendly and are primarily intended for direct use by developers to perform common version control tasks. results.question: Describe the Integration-Manager workflow commonly used with tools like GitHub.
results.expected_answer: In this workflow, every developer has write access to their own public fork and read access to the main canonical repository. They push changes to their fork and then send a pull request to the maintainer, who tests and merges the changes into the main project.
results.rtfm_answer: The Integration-Manager workflow, commonly used with tools like GitHub or GitLab, involves contributors pushing changes to their own public repositories and then notifying the maintainer via email. The maintainer then merges these changes into the main repository. This allows contributors to work independently while the maintainer can integrate changes at their convenience. [Source 1]

results.question: What is a topic branch and why is it used?
results.expected_answer: A topic branch is a short-lived branch created for a single particular feature or bug fix. This technique allows developers to context-switch quickly and keep work isolated in silos until it is ready for code review and merging.
results.rtfm_answer: A topic branch is a short-lived branch used for a single particular feature or related work. It allows for quick and complete context-switching, making it easier to manage changes and perform code reviews. This approach is particularly useful in projects of any size, especially those that are large or complex, as it helps keep changes organized and manageable.

results.question: How does the Benevolent Dictator workflow operate for very large projects?
results.expected_answer: This hierarchical workflow involves 'lieutenants' who merge developers' topic branches and a 'dictator' who merges lieutenants' work into a master branch. Finally, the dictator pushes that master branch to a blessed reference repository for all others to use.
results.rtfm_answer: In the Benevolent Dictator workflow for very large projects, regular developers work on their topic branches and rebase their work on top of the master branch, which is managed by the reference repository. Lieutenants merge the developers' topic branches into their master branch. The dictator then merges the lieutenants' master branches into the dictator’s master branch and finally pushes this master branch to the reference repository, allowing other developers to rebase on it. This workflow is useful in highly hierarchical environments or very big projects where the project leader can delegate work and integrate code at multiple points.
